fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
This sentence is by the decree of the watchers, the verdict by the word of the holy ones, so that everyone living may know that the Most High rules over human kingdoms and gives them to anyone he chooses, and even sets over them the lowliest of people.’

— Daniel 4:17

Daniel is two books in one. The first half is made of stories that children learn before they can read: four young men who will not eat the king’s food, three friends in a blazing furnace, a hand writing on a palace wall, an old man thrown to the lions. The second half is made of visions that have puzzled scholars for two thousand years: four beasts rising out of the sea, a ram and a goat, seventy sevens, and a long and detailed account of kings of the north and the south. Both halves say the same thing. Empires rise and fall, and some of them set themselves against God and his people, but “the Most High rules over human kingdoms”, and his kingdom will never be destroyed.

Its hero is a young man of Judah taken to Babylon, who spends his whole life serving pagan kings without ever ceasing to serve his God. Daniel’s name means “God is my judge”, and the book shows a man who lived as if that were true, in a palace where every other judge was hostile.

Two halves, two languages

The book divides into two halves of six chapters each:

  • Chapters 1–6: stories of Daniel and his friends at the courts of Babylon and Persia, told mostly in the third person.
  • Chapters 7–12: four visions given to Daniel, told mostly in his own voice, reaching from his own day to “the time of the end”.

It also divides another way. Daniel is written in two languages. It begins in Hebrew, switches in the middle of 2:4, when the king’s advisers speak to him “in Aramaic”, the common language of the empire, and stays in Aramaic until the end of chapter 7, before returning to Hebrew for the rest. The Aramaic chapters form a pattern of their own: a dream of four kingdoms (2) and a vision of four kingdoms (7) on the outside; two rescues of the faithful, from the furnace (3) and from the lions (6); and at the centre, two proud kings judged (4 and 5). The book is more carefully built than it first looks.

In the Hebrew Bible, Daniel stands among the Writings, with Psalms, Esther and Ezra, rather than among the Prophets. In Christian Bibles, following the ancient Greek translation, it comes after Ezekiel as the last of the major prophets. The Greek also included additional passages, the prayer of the three young men in the furnace and the stories of Susanna and of Bel and the Dragon, which Catholic and Orthodox Bibles keep; this translation, made from the Hebrew and Aramaic, does not include them.

Faithful in Babylon (Daniel 1)

The book opens in 605 BC, “in the third year of Jehoiakim’s reign”, when Nebuchadnezzar comes to Jerusalem and carries off young men of the royal family and the nobility to be trained for his service. Among them are Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, renamed Belteshazzar, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego. They are given a Babylonian education, Babylonian names, and food from the king’s table.

They accept the education and the names. They draw the line at the food: “Daniel resolved not to make himself unclean with the royal food or with the wine the king drank.” He does not rebel or make a scene; he proposes a ten-day test, vegetables and water, and the four come out healthier than everyone else. At the end of their training the king finds them “ten times wiser than all the magicians and enchanters in his entire kingdom.” The chapter is a pattern for living faithfully in a culture that is not your own: learn its language, serve it well, and know where you will not bend.

Its last verse quietly spans the whole book: “Daniel remained there until the first year of King Cyrus.” He outlived the empire that took him.

The statue and the stone (Daniel 2)

Nebuchadnezzar has a dream that troubles him, and demands that his wise men tell him not only what it means but what it was. They protest that no one on earth could do such a thing. Daniel and his friends pray, the mystery is revealed to Daniel in a vision at night, and his first response is praise:

Daniel said: “Blessed be the name of God from age to age, for wisdom and power belong to him. He changes times and seasons; he deposes kings and installs kings. He gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those with insight.

— Daniel 2:20–21

The king had seen a great statue: a head of gold, chest and arms of silver, belly and thighs of bronze, legs of iron, and feet partly of iron and partly of clay. A stone “cut out, though no human hand touched it” struck its feet, and the whole statue crumbled like chaff and blew away, while the stone “grew into a great mountain and filled the whole earth.” Daniel explains: “You are the head of gold.” Other kingdoms will follow, each lesser than the last, and then the God of heaven will set up “a kingdom that will never be destroyed.”

The furnace (Daniel 3)

Nebuchadnezzar sets up a gold statue on the plain of Dura and commands everyone to bow down to it when the music plays, on pain of the furnace. Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego will not. Brought before the furious king, they give one of the great answers of faith in the Bible:

If it comes to that, our God whom we serve is able to rescue us from the blazing furnace, and he will rescue us from your power, O king. But even if he does not, you must know, O king, that we will not serve your gods, nor will we worship the gold statue you have set up.”

— Daniel 3:17–18

“But even if he does not.” Their obedience does not depend on rescue. They are thrown into a furnace so hot that it kills the men who throw them in. And the king, looking in, jumps to his feet: “Look! I see four men, untied, walking around in the fire, and they are unharmed! And the fourth looks like a son of the gods.” The fire has burned only their ropes. Nebuchadnezzar can only call the fourth figure an angel; Christian readers from the early centuries on have wondered whether it was the Son of God himself, walking with his people in the fire.

Two proud kings (Daniel 4–5)

Chapter 4 is told by Nebuchadnezzar himself, as a letter to all peoples. He dreams of a great tree cut down, and Daniel warns him that it is a picture of himself, and pleads with him to break with his sins “by showing mercy to the oppressed”. A year later, walking on his palace roof, the king boasts, “Is this not the great Babylon that I have built as a royal capital by my own mighty power and for the glory of my majesty?” At that moment his mind is taken from him, and he lives like an animal in the fields until he looks up to heaven and his sanity returns. The king who would be worshipped ends his letter in worship: “Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and exalt and honor the King of heaven… and he can bring down those who live in pride.”

Belshazzar does not learn the lesson. At a great feast he drinks from the gold and silver vessels taken from the temple in Jerusalem, and praises the gods of gold and silver. The fingers of a human hand appear and write on the wall. Daniel, now an old man, is brought in, and reads the words: MENE, MENE, TEKEL and PARSIN. God has numbered the days of his kingdom; “you have been weighed on the scales and found too light”; his kingdom is given to the Medes and Persians. “That very night Belshazzar, king of the Chaldeans, was killed.” Babylon fell to Cyrus in 539 BC.

Belshazzar was long unknown outside the Bible, until inscriptions were found naming him as the eldest son of Nabonidus, the last king of Babylon, who left him to rule in the city while he himself was away for years. That is why Belshazzar could offer Daniel no more than to be “the third ruler in the kingdom”.

The lions’ den (Daniel 6)

Under the new ruler, Darius the Mede, Daniel rises so high that the other officials look for a charge against him and find none, except in “the law of his God”. They persuade the king to sign a decree that for thirty days no one may pray to any god or human being except the king. Daniel’s response is simply to go on as before:

When Daniel learned that the decree had been signed, he went home to his upstairs room, where the windows opened toward Jerusalem. Three times a day he got down on his knees and prayed, giving thanks to his God, just as he had always done.

— Daniel 6:10

He prays toward Jerusalem, as Solomon had asked exiles to do (1 Kings 8:48), though the city and its temple lie in ruins. He is thrown to the lions, and the king, who cannot undo his own law, spends the night without food or sleep. At dawn he runs to the den and calls out in anguish, and hears the old man answer: “My God sent his angel and shut the lions’ mouths.” Darius ends the story, as Nebuchadnezzar ended his, by praising “the living God, who endures forever”, whose “kingdom will never be destroyed.”

Who Darius the Mede was is still discussed. He is not named outside the Bible, and scholars have identified him with Cyrus himself, with a governor under Cyrus, or with others; some think the book uses a traditional figure. What the story asks of its reader is clear either way.

The beasts and the son of man (Daniel 7)

The second half of the book turns from stories to visions. In the first year of Belshazzar, Daniel dreams of four beasts rising from a stormy sea: a lion with eagle’s wings, a bear with ribs in its mouth, a four-headed leopard, and a fourth beast “terrifying, frightening and very strong”, with iron teeth and ten horns, among which a small horn grows up “and a mouth that spoke boastfully.” Then the scene changes to a courtroom in heaven. Thrones are set, “and the Ancient of Days was seated”, his clothes white as snow, his throne a flame of fire. The beast is destroyed. And then:

As I watched in the visions of the night, I saw one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven. He came to the Ancient of Days and was presented before him. He was given authority, glory and kingly power, so that all peoples, nations and languages would serve him. His authority is an everlasting authority that will never pass away, and his kingdom will never be destroyed.

— Daniel 7:13–14

The beasts rise from the sea, the Bible’s picture of chaos; the one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven, from God. Human empires are bestial; God’s kingdom is truly human. The angel explains that the kingdom will be given to “the holy ones of the Most High”, who will possess it forever.

No passage in Daniel matters more to the New Testament. “The Son of Man” was the name Jesus used most often for himself, and at his trial, asked by the high priest if he was the Messiah, he answered: “I am. And you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven” (Mark 14:62). The high priest tore his clothes.

Rams, goats and seventy sevens (Daniel 8–12)

The remaining visions narrow their focus. In chapter 8 a two-horned ram is trampled by a goat with a great horn; the angel Gabriel explains that they are the kings of Media and Persia and the king of Greece, and from the goat comes a horn that grows great, stops the daily offering and throws down the sanctuary. In chapters 10–12 a heavenly messenger describes, in remarkable detail, the wars of the kings of the north and the south after the Greek empire divided. Many details fit closely the history of the second century BC, and of Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who outlawed the Jewish faith and set up an altar to Zeus in the temple in 167 BC, “the abomination that brings ruin.”

Between these comes Daniel’s great prayer in chapter 9. Reading Jeremiah, he understands that the desolation of Jerusalem is to last seventy years, and the years are nearly done. He does not wait. He fasts and prays in sackcloth and ashes, confessing his people’s sin as his own: “We have sinned and done wrong.” He asks not on the basis of their righteousness “but because of your great mercy”. Gabriel comes “about the hour of the evening offering”, though no offering had been made for decades, and tells him that “Seventy sevens have been decreed”, to put an end to sin and “to bring in everlasting righteousness”, with “an anointed one” who “will be cut off”.

The book ends with one of the clearest promises of resurrection in the Old Testament: “Many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, these to everlasting life, and those to shame and everlasting contempt.” And it ends with Daniel himself, who does not understand all he has seen, told to “go your way until the end”, with the promise that he will rise.

When was Daniel written?

Christians disagree about the date of the book, and the question is bound up with how the visions are read. The traditional view, held by Jewish and Christian readers for most of history and by many today, is that the book comes from Daniel himself in the sixth century BC, and that its detailed visions are true predictive prophecy. Many scholars date the final form of the book to the 160s BC, during the persecution under Antiochus, holding that older stories of Daniel were joined to visions written to encourage the faithful in that crisis. Others take mediating positions. Readers on every side agree that the book was written to strengthen God’s people under hostile powers, and that it has done so ever since.

The visions themselves have also been read in different ways. The four kingdoms of chapters 2 and 7 have traditionally been taken as Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome, with God’s kingdom arriving in Christ; many modern interpreters count Babylon, Media, Persia and Greece. The seventy sevens of chapter 9 have been calculated to the coming and death of the Messiah, to the time of Antiochus, and to a final period at the end of history. Readers should hold these schemes humbly. The book itself says that Daniel was “dismayed by the vision; it was beyond understanding.”

How to read Daniel

Read the stories first, and read them as stories: they are told with great skill and humour, and they teach courage by showing it. Notice that in every one God’s people are under pressure from a power far greater than they are, and that God’s rescue sometimes comes and sometimes is only trusted for: “even if he does not.”

Then read the visions as the stories told again in another key. The kings who demand worship become beasts; the furnace and the den become persecution on a vast scale; and the end is the same, a kingdom given by God that will never be destroyed. Do not let the puzzles of the numbers keep you from the plain message: history is in God’s hands, the arrogant will fall, and those who stay faithful will “shine like the brightness of the sky”.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and Aramaic and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The prayers and visions that are poetry in the original are printed one line per line. A few of its choices are worth knowing.

“One like a son of man.” The Aramaic phrase in 7:13 is kept as “one like a son of man”, a figure who looks human, so that readers can see the phrase that Jesus took up as his own title.

“The Most High.” The title by which Daniel and even the pagan kings speak of God is kept throughout, and so is the vivid name of Daniel 7, “the Ancient of Days”.

“The abomination that brings ruin.” The phrase from 9:27, 11:31 and 12:11, older Bibles’ “abomination of desolation”, is rendered “the abomination that brings ruin”, the same words used where Jesus speaks “of which the prophet Daniel spoke” (Matthew 24:15).

Units. Measures are given in modern terms, so that Nebuchadnezzar’s statue is “about 90 feet high and about 9 feet wide”.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew and Aramaic beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Daniel 1
fields.body_html:
Daniel and his friends in Babylon

In the third year of Jehoiakim’s reign as king of Judah, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and laid siege to it. The Lord handed Jehoiakim king of Judah over to him, along with some of the vessels from the house of God. He carried them off to the land of Shinar, to the temple of his god, and put the vessels in the treasury of his god. Then the king ordered Ashpenaz, his chief court officer, to bring in some of the Israelites from the royal family and from the nobility, young men without any defect, good-looking, skilled in every kind of wisdom, well informed and quick to learn, able to serve in the king’s palace. He was to teach them the literature and language of the Chaldeans. The king assigned them a daily ration from the royal food and from the wine he drank. They were to be trained for three years, and after that they were to enter the king’s service. Among these, from the people of Judah, were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah. The chief court officer gave them new names: he called Daniel Belteshazzar, Hananiah Shadrach, Mishael Meshach, and Azariah Abednego. But Daniel resolved not to make himself unclean with the royal food or with the wine the king drank, and he asked the chief court officer for permission not to make himself unclean. Now God had caused the chief court officer to show Daniel kindness and compassion. But the chief court officer said to Daniel, “I am afraid of my lord the king. He is the one who assigned your food and drink. What if he sees that you look worse than the other young men your age? You would put my head at risk with the king.” So Daniel spoke to the guard whom the chief court officer had put in charge of Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah. “Please test your servants for ten days: let us be given vegetables to eat and water to drink. Then compare our appearance with the appearance of the young men who eat the royal food, and then treat your servants in the light of what you see.” So he agreed to this and tested them for ten days. At the end of the ten days they looked healthier and better fed than any of the young men who ate the royal food. So the guard took away the royal food and the wine they were supposed to drink, and gave them vegetables instead. To these four young men God gave knowledge and skill in every kind of literature and wisdom, and Daniel could understand visions and dreams of every kind. At the end of the time the king had set for bringing them in, the chief court officer presented them to Nebuchadnezzar. The king talked with them, and among them all there was no one like Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah. So they entered the king’s service. In every matter of wisdom and understanding that the king asked them about, he found them ten times wiser than all the magicians and enchanters in his entire kingdom. And Daniel remained there until the first year of King Cyrus.

fields.title: Daniel 2
fields.body_html:
Nebuchadnezzar’s dream

In the second year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign, Nebuchadnezzar had dreams. His mind was so troubled that he could not sleep. So the king ordered that the magicians, enchanters, sorcerers and Chaldeans be summoned to tell the king what he had dreamed. They came and stood before the king. The king said to them, “I have had a dream, and my mind is troubled. I want to know what the dream was.” Then the Chaldeans spoke to the king in Aramaic, “O king, may you live forever! Describe the dream to your servants, and we will explain its meaning.” The king replied to the Chaldeans, “My decision is firm: unless you tell me both the dream and its interpretation, you will be torn limb from limb, and your houses will be turned into rubbish heaps. But if you make known the dream and its interpretation, you will receive gifts and rewards and great honor from me. So tell me the dream and its interpretation.” They answered a second time, “Let the king tell his servants the dream, and we will make known its interpretation.” The king replied, “I know for sure that you are trying to gain time, because you see that my decision is final. If you do not make the dream known to me, there is just one sentence for you. You have agreed among yourselves to tell me lies and deceit until things change. So tell me the dream, and then I will know that you can explain it to me.” The Chaldeans answered the king, “There is no one on earth who can do what the king asks! No king, however great and powerful, has ever asked such a thing of any magician, enchanter or Chaldean. What the king asks is too difficult. No one can reveal it to the king except the gods, and they do not live among human beings.” This made the king so angry and furious that he ordered all the wise men of Babylon to be put to death. So the decree was issued that the wise men were to be killed, and they looked for Daniel and his friends to kill them.

Daniel asks for time

Then Daniel spoke with wisdom and tact to Arioch, the commander of the king’s guard, who had gone out to put the wise men of Babylon to death. He asked Arioch, the king’s officer, “Why is the king’s decree so urgent?” Then Arioch explained the matter to Daniel. So Daniel went in and asked the king to give him time, so that he might tell the king the interpretation.

The secret revealed to Daniel

Then Daniel went home and told his friends Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah what had happened.
He urged them to ask the God of heaven for mercy concerning this mystery, so that he and his friends would not be put to death with the rest of the wise men of Babylon.
Then the mystery was revealed to Daniel in a vision during the night, and Daniel praised the God of heaven.
Daniel said:
“Blessed be the name of God
from age to age,
for wisdom and power belong to him.
He changes times and seasons;
he deposes kings and installs kings.
He gives wisdom to the wise
and knowledge to those with insight.
He reveals deep and hidden things;
he knows what is in the darkness,
and light lives with him.
To you, God of my ancestors, I give thanks and praise,
for you have given me wisdom and power.
Now you have shown me what we asked of you;
you have made known to us what the king wanted to know.”
So Daniel went to Arioch, whom the king had appointed to put the wise men of Babylon to death. He went and said to him, “Do not put the wise men of Babylon to death. Take me to the king, and I will tell the king the interpretation.”

Daniel before the king

Arioch quickly took Daniel to the king and said, “I have found a man among the exiles from Judah who can tell the king the interpretation.” The king said to Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, “Can you tell me the dream I had and what it means?” Daniel replied to the king, “No wise men, enchanters, magicians or diviners can explain to the king the mystery he has asked about. But there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries. He has shown King Nebuchadnezzar what will happen in the days to come. This was your dream, the visions that passed through your mind as you lay in bed:

The statue and the stone

As you lay in bed, O king, your thoughts turned to what would happen in the future, and the revealer of mysteries has shown you what is going to happen. As for me, this mystery has not been revealed to me because I have more wisdom than anyone else alive, but so that the king may know the interpretation and understand the thoughts of his heart. You were watching, O king, and there before you stood a great statue. This statue was huge and its brightness dazzling, and it stood in front of you, frightening to look at. The head of the statue was made of fine gold, its chest and arms of silver, its belly and thighs of bronze, its legs of iron, and its feet partly of iron and partly of baked clay. While you watched, a stone was cut out, though no human hand touched it. It struck the statue’s feet of iron and clay and smashed them. Then the iron, the clay, the bronze, the silver and the gold were all broken to pieces at once and became like chaff on a threshing floor in summer. The wind swept them away, and not a trace of them remained. But the stone that had struck the statue grew into a great mountain and filled the whole earth. That was the dream. Now we will tell the king its interpretation. You, O king, are the king of kings. The God of heaven has given you the kingdom, the power, the might and the glory. Wherever people live, he has put them in your power, and the wild animals and the birds of the sky too, and he has made you ruler over them all. You are the head of gold. After you another kingdom will arise, inferior to yours, and then a third kingdom, of bronze, which will rule over the whole earth. Then there will be a fourth kingdom, strong as iron. Just as iron shatters and crushes everything, and as iron breaks things to pieces, it will crush and break all the others. And just as you saw that the feet and toes were partly potter’s clay and partly iron, so it will be a divided kingdom. It will still have some of the strength of iron, as you saw iron mixed with clay. The toes of the feet were part iron and part clay; so the kingdom will be partly strong and partly brittle. And as you saw iron mixed with clay, so they will mix with one another by marriage, but they will not hold together, just as iron does not mix with clay. In the time of those kings the God of heaven will establish a kingdom that will never be destroyed. Its rule will never pass to another people. It will crush all these kingdoms and bring them to an end, but it will itself endure forever. This is the meaning of the stone you saw cut out of the mountain, not by human hands, which smashed the iron, the bronze, the clay, the silver and the gold. A great God has shown the king what is to come. The dream is certain, and its interpretation can be trusted.”

The king honors Daniel

Then King Nebuchadnezzar fell face down and bowed before Daniel, and he ordered that an offering and incense be presented to him. The king said to Daniel, “Your God is truly the God above all gods and the Lord over kings, and one who reveals mysteries, for you have been able to reveal this mystery.” Then the king promoted Daniel and gave him many great gifts. He made him ruler over the whole province of Babylon and chief prefect in charge of all the wise men of Babylon. Daniel made a request of the king, and the king put Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in charge of the affairs of the province of Babylon, while Daniel remained at the royal court.

fields.title: Daniel 3
fields.body_html:
The gold statue

King Nebuchadnezzar made a gold statue about 90 feet high and about 9 feet wide, and he had it set up on the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon. Then King Nebuchadnezzar sent word to gather the satraps, the prefects, the governors, the counselors, the treasurers, the judges, the magistrates and all the officials of the provinces to come to the dedication of the statue that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up. So the satraps, the prefects, the governors, the counselors, the treasurers, the judges, the magistrates and all the officials of the provinces gathered for the dedication of the statue King Nebuchadnezzar had set up. They stood in front of the statue Nebuchadnezzar had set up. Then the herald called out loudly, “Peoples, nations and people of every language, this is the command to you: As soon as you hear the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe and every kind of music, you must fall down and worship the gold statue that King Nebuchadnezzar has set up. Anyone who does not fall down and worship will immediately be thrown into a blazing furnace.” So as soon as all the peoples heard the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp and every kind of music, all the peoples, nations and people of every language fell down and worshiped the gold statue that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up. Then at that time some Chaldeans came forward and brought malicious charges against the Jews. They said to King Nebuchadnezzar, “O king, may you live forever! You, O king, have made a decree: everyone who hears the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe and every kind of music must fall down and worship the gold statue, and that anyone who does not fall down and worship will be thrown into a blazing furnace. There are some Jews, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, whom you have put in charge of the affairs of the province of Babylon. These men pay no attention to you, O king. They do not serve your gods or worship the gold statue you have set up.”

Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego before the king

Then Nebuchadnezzar, in a furious rage, ordered that Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego be brought in. So these men were brought before the king. Nebuchadnezzar said to them, “Is it true, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, that you do not serve my gods or worship the gold statue I have set up? Now then, if you are ready to fall down and worship the statue I have made when you hear the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe and every kind of music, very well. But if you do not worship, you will immediately be thrown into a blazing furnace. And what god is there who can rescue you from my power?” Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego replied to the king, “Nebuchadnezzar, we do not need to defend ourselves before you in this matter. If it comes to that, our God whom we serve is able to rescue us from the blazing furnace, and he will rescue us from your power, O king. But even if he does not, you must know, O king, that we will not serve your gods, nor will we worship the gold statue you have set up.”

The blazing furnace

Then Nebuchadnezzar was filled with rage, and his expression changed toward Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego. He ordered the furnace heated seven times hotter than it was normally heated. He commanded some of the strongest soldiers of his army to tie up Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego and to throw them into the blazing furnace. So these men were tied up, still wearing their trousers, their tunics, their caps and their other clothes, and they were thrown into the blazing furnace. Because the king’s order was so urgent and the furnace so very hot, the flames of the fire killed the men who carried Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego up to it. And these three men, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, fell, still tied up, into the blazing furnace.

Four men in the fire

Then King Nebuchadnezzar was amazed, and he jumped to his feet. He asked his advisers, “Did we not throw three men, tied up, into the fire?” They replied to the king, “Yes, O king, we did.” He said, “Look! I see four men, untied, walking around in the fire, and they are unharmed! And the fourth looks like a son of the gods.”

Out of the fire

Then Nebuchadnezzar went up to the opening of the blazing furnace and called, “Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, servants of the Most High God, step out and come here!” So Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego came out of the fire. The satraps, prefects, governors and the king’s advisers crowded around and saw that the fire had had no power over the bodies of these men. The hair of their heads was not singed, their trousers were not scorched, and there was no smell of fire on them. Nebuchadnezzar said, “Praise be to the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, who sent his angel and rescued his servants! They trusted in him, defied the king’s command and were willing to give up their lives rather than serve or bow down to any god but their own. So I issue this decree: any people, nation or language that says anything against the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego will be torn limb from limb and their houses turned into rubbish heaps. For there is no other god who can rescue like this.” Then the king gave Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego higher positions in the province of Babylon.

fields.title: Daniel 4
fields.body_html:
Nebuchadnezzar’s letter

From King Nebuchadnezzar, to all the peoples, nations and people of every language who live in all the earth: May you have abundant peace!
I am pleased to make known to you
the signs and wonders that the Most High God has done for me.

The dream of the great tree

How great are his signs!
How powerful are his wonders!
His kingdom is a kingdom for all ages;
his rule lasts through every generation.
I, Nebuchadnezzar, was living at ease in my house, prospering in my palace.
I had a dream that frightened me. As I lay in bed, the images and visions that passed through my mind terrified me.
So I gave orders for all the wise men of Babylon to be brought before me to tell me what the dream meant.
Then the magicians, enchanters, Chaldeans and diviners came in, and I told them the dream, but they could not tell me what it meant.
At last Daniel came in before me. He is called Belteshazzar, after the name of my god, and the spirit of the holy gods is in him. I told him the dream:
“Belteshazzar, chief of the magicians, I am sure that the spirit of the holy gods is within you and that no mystery is too hard for you. Here are the visions I saw in my dream; tell me what they mean.
These were the visions that passed through my mind as I lay in bed: I looked, and there before me was a tree in the middle of the earth, and it was very tall.
The tree grew large and strong; its top touched the sky, and it could be seen from the ends of the earth.
Its leaves were beautiful and its fruit plentiful, and on it was food for everyone. Wild animals rested in its shade, birds nested in its branches, and every living creature was fed from it.
As I lay in bed, I was watching the visions in my mind, and there before me was a watcher, a holy one, coming down from heaven.
He shouted in a loud voice: ‘Fell the tree and lop off its branches; strip away its leaves and scatter its fruit. Let the animals flee from under it and the birds from its branches.
But leave the stump with its roots in the ground, bound with a band of iron and bronze, in the grass of the field. Let him be soaked with the dew of heaven, and let him share the lot of the animals in the grass of the earth.
Let his mind be changed from that of a human being, and let him be given the mind of an animal, until seven periods of time pass over him.
This sentence is by the decree of the watchers, the verdict by the word of the holy ones, so that everyone living may know that the Most High rules over human kingdoms and gives them to anyone he chooses, and even sets over them the lowliest of people.’
This is the dream that I, King Nebuchadnezzar, had. Now, Belteshazzar, tell me what it means, for none of the wise men of my kingdom can explain it to me. But you can, because the spirit of the holy gods is in you.”
Then Daniel, also called Belteshazzar, was dismayed for a while, and his thoughts frightened him. The king said, “Belteshazzar, do not let the dream or its meaning frighten you.” Belteshazzar answered, “My lord, if only the dream were about those who hate you, and its meaning about your enemies!
The tree you saw, which grew large and strong, whose top touched the sky and which could be seen by the whole earth,
whose leaves were beautiful and its fruit plentiful, providing food for all, under which the wild animals lived and in whose branches the birds of the sky nested,
that tree is you, O king! You have grown great and strong; your greatness has grown until it reaches the sky, and your rule extends to the ends of the earth.
And as for the watcher, a holy one, whom the king saw coming down from heaven and saying, ‘Fell the tree and destroy it, but leave its stump and roots in the ground, bound with a band of iron and bronze, in the grass of the field. Let him be soaked with the dew of heaven, and let him share the lot of the wild animals until seven periods of time pass over him,’
this is what it means, O king, and it is the decree of the Most High that has come upon my lord the king:
You will be driven away from people and will live with the wild animals. You will be made to eat grass like cattle, and you will be drenched with the dew of heaven. Seven periods of time will pass over you, until you acknowledge that the Most High rules over human kingdoms and gives them to anyone he chooses.
The order to leave the tree’s stump and roots means that your kingdom will be given back to you as soon as you acknowledge that Heaven rules.
Therefore, O king, please accept my advice: break with your sins by doing what is right, and with your wrongs by showing mercy to the oppressed. Perhaps then your prosperity will continue.”
All this happened to King Nebuchadnezzar.

The king is humbled and restored

Twelve months later, as he was strolling on the roof of the royal palace of Babylon,
the king said, “Is this not the great Babylon that I have built as a royal capital by my own mighty power and for the glory of my majesty?”
The words were still on the king’s lips when a voice came down from heaven: “King Nebuchadnezzar, this is decreed for you: your kingdom has been taken from you.
You will be driven away from people to live with the wild animals. You will be made to eat grass like cattle, and seven periods of time will pass over you, until you acknowledge that the Most High rules over human kingdoms and gives them to anyone he chooses.”
At that very moment the word was fulfilled against Nebuchadnezzar. He was driven away from people and ate grass like cattle, and his body was soaked with the dew of heaven, until his hair grew as long as eagles’ feathers and his nails like the claws of birds.
At the end of that time, I, Nebuchadnezzar, looked up to heaven, and my sanity was restored.
Then I blessed the Most High;
I praised and honored the one who lives forever.
His rule is an everlasting rule,
and his kingdom lasts through every generation.
All the people of the earth count as nothing before him;
he does as he pleases with the armies of heaven
and with the people of the earth.
No one can hold back his hand
or say to him, “What have you done?”
At that same time my sanity returned, and my majesty and splendor came back to me, to the glory of my kingdom. My advisers and nobles came looking for me; I was set over my kingdom again, and still greater power was given to me.
Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and exalt and honor the King of heaven, because everything he does is right and his ways are just, and he can bring down those who live in pride.

fields.title: Daniel 5
fields.body_html:
Belshazzar’s feast

King Belshazzar gave a great banquet for a thousand of his nobles, and he drank wine in front of them all. While Belshazzar was tasting the wine, he ordered that the gold and silver vessels his father Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple in Jerusalem be brought in, so that the king and his nobles, his wives and his concubines could drink from them. So the gold vessels that had been carried off from the temple, the house of God in Jerusalem, were brought in, and the king and his nobles, his wives and his concubines drank from them. They drank the wine and praised the gods of gold and silver, of bronze, iron, wood and stone. At that very moment the fingers of a human hand appeared and began writing on the plaster of the palace wall, across from the lampstand. The king watched the hand as it wrote. Then the king turned pale. His thoughts terrified him, his legs gave way, and his knees knocked together. The king shouted for the enchanters, Chaldeans and diviners to be brought in. The king said to the wise men of Babylon, “Anyone who can read this writing and tell me what it means will be dressed in purple and have a gold chain around his neck, and he will be the third ruler in the kingdom.”

The wise men fail

Then all the king’s wise men came in, but none of them could read the writing or tell the king what it meant. Then King Belshazzar became even more terrified and his face grew pale, and his nobles were bewildered. The queen, hearing the voices of the king and his nobles, came into the banquet hall. The queen said, “O king, may you live forever! Do not be alarmed, and do not let your face grow pale. In your kingdom there is a man in whom the spirit of the holy gods lives. In your father’s time he showed insight, understanding and wisdom like the wisdom of the gods. Your father, King Nebuchadnezzar, made him chief of the magicians, enchanters, Chaldeans and diviners. Yes, your father the king did this, because this Daniel, whom the king named Belteshazzar, was found to have an extraordinary spirit, knowledge and understanding to interpret dreams, explain riddles and solve hard problems. So now let Daniel be called, and he will tell you what the writing means.”

Daniel before Belshazzar

So Daniel was brought in before the king, and the king said to him, “Are you that Daniel, one of the exiles from Judah, whom my father the king brought from Judah? I have heard about you: the spirit of the gods is in you, and you have insight, understanding and extraordinary wisdom. The wise men and enchanters were brought in before me to read this writing and tell me what it means, but they could not explain it. But I have heard that you can give interpretations and solve hard problems. Now if you can read this writing and tell me what it means, you will be dressed in purple and have a gold chain around your neck, and you will be the third ruler in the kingdom.”

Daniel reads the writing

Then Daniel answered the king, “You may keep your gifts and give your rewards to someone else. Still, I will read the writing for the king and tell him what it means. O king, the Most High God gave your father Nebuchadnezzar the kingdom, greatness, glory and majesty. Because of the greatness he gave him, all the peoples, nations and people of every language trembled and were afraid of him. He put to death anyone he wanted to, and let live anyone he wanted to. He raised up anyone he wanted to, and humbled anyone he wanted to. But when his heart became proud and his spirit hardened in arrogance, he was brought down from his royal throne and his glory was stripped from him. He was driven away from people, and his mind was made like that of an animal. He lived with the wild donkeys and was fed grass like cattle, and his body was soaked with the dew of heaven, until he came to know that the Most High God rules over human kingdoms and sets over them anyone he chooses. But you, Belshazzar, his son, have not humbled yourself, even though you knew all this. Instead, you have set yourself up against the Lord of heaven. You had the vessels from his house brought to you, and you and your nobles, your wives and your concubines drank wine from them. You praised gods of silver and gold, of bronze, iron, wood and stone, which neither see nor hear nor understand. Yet you have not honored the God who holds your life in his hand and controls everything you do. That is why he sent the hand that wrote this inscription. This is the writing that was inscribed: MENE, MENE, TEKEL and PARSIN. This is what the words mean: MENE: God has numbered the days of your kingdom and brought it to an end. TEKEL: you have been weighed on the scales and found too light. PERES: your kingdom has been divided and given to the Medes and Persians.” Then at Belshazzar’s command Daniel was dressed in purple, a gold chain was put around his neck, and it was proclaimed that he would be the third ruler in the kingdom. That very night Belshazzar, king of the Chaldeans, was killed.

And Darius the Mede took over the kingdom when he was about sixty-two years old.

fields.title: Daniel 6
fields.body_html:
Daniel and the officials of Darius

Darius decided to appoint 120 satraps to rule throughout the kingdom, and over them three high officials, one of whom was Daniel. The satraps were to report to them, so that the king would not suffer loss. Now Daniel distinguished himself above the other high officials and the satraps because of the extraordinary spirit in him, and the king planned to set him over the whole kingdom. So the high officials and the satraps tried to find grounds for a charge against Daniel in his conduct of government affairs, but they could find no grounds and no corruption, because he was trustworthy; no negligence or corruption could be found in him. Then these men said, “We will never find any grounds for a charge against this Daniel unless it has to do with the law of his God.”

The king’s ban

So these high officials and satraps went as a group to the king and said to him, “King Darius, may you live forever! All the high officials of the kingdom, the prefects and satraps, the advisers and governors, have agreed that the king should issue a decree and enforce a ban: anyone who prays to any god or human being for the next thirty days, except to you, O king, will be thrown into the lions’ den. Now, O king, issue the ban and sign it in writing, so that it cannot be changed, as is the law of the Medes and Persians, which cannot be repealed.” So King Darius signed the written ban. When Daniel learned that the decree had been signed, he went home to his upstairs room, where the windows opened toward Jerusalem. Three times a day he got down on his knees and prayed, giving thanks to his God, just as he had always done.

Daniel in the lions’ den

Then these men went as a group and found Daniel praying and asking his God for help.
So they went to the king and spoke to him about his ban: “O king, did you not sign a ban saying that anyone who prays to any god or human being for thirty days, except to you, would be thrown into the lions’ den?” The king answered, “That decree stands, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which cannot be repealed.”
Then they said to the king, “Daniel, one of the exiles from Judah, pays no attention to you, O king, or to the ban you signed. He still prays three times a day.”
When the king heard this, he was deeply distressed. He was determined to save Daniel, and until sunset he tried everything he could to rescue him.
Then these men went as a group to the king and said, “Do not forget, O king, that under the law of the Medes and Persians no ban or decree the king issues can be changed.”
So the king gave the order, and Daniel was brought and thrown into the lions’ den. The king said to Daniel, “May your God, whom you serve faithfully, rescue you!”
Then a stone was brought and set over the opening of the den. The king sealed it with his own ring and with the rings of his nobles, so that Daniel’s sentence could not be changed.
Then the king went back to his palace and spent the night without eating. He allowed no entertainment to be brought to him, and he could not sleep.
At daybreak, as soon as it was light, the king rose and went in haste to the lions’ den.
When he came near the den, he called out to Daniel in an anguished voice, “Daniel, servant of the living God! Has your God, whom you faithfully serve, been able to rescue you from the lions?”
Then Daniel answered the king, “O king, may you live forever!
My God sent his angel and shut the lions’ mouths, and they have not hurt me, because I was found innocent in his sight. And I have done nothing wrong before you either, O king.”
The king was overjoyed and ordered that Daniel be lifted out of the den. So Daniel was lifted out, and no injury of any kind was found on him, because he had trusted in his God.
Then at the king’s command the men who had falsely accused Daniel were brought in and thrown into the lions’ den, together with their children and their wives. They had not yet reached the floor of the den when the lions overpowered them and broke all their bones.
Then King Darius wrote to all the peoples, nations and people of every language who live in all the earth: “May you have abundant peace!
I decree that in every part of my kingdom
people must tremble with fear
before the God of Daniel,
because he is the living God, who endures forever;
his kingdom will never be destroyed,
and his rule will never end.
He saves and rescues; he does signs and wonders
in heaven and on earth.
He has rescued Daniel
from the power of the lions.”
So Daniel prospered during the reigns of Darius and of Cyrus the Persian.

fields.title: Daniel 7
fields.body_html:
Four beasts from the sea

In the first year of Belshazzar’s reign over Babylon, Daniel had a dream, and as he lay in bed, visions came into his mind. Then he wrote the dream down and gave an account of the main things in it.
Daniel said: In my vision at night I looked, and I saw the four winds of heaven churning up the great sea.
Four huge beasts rose out of the sea, each unlike the others.
The first was like a lion, and it had eagle’s wings. As I watched, its wings were torn off, and it was lifted from the ground and set on two feet like a human being, and it was given a human mind.
Then I saw another beast, a second one, that looked like a bear. It was raised up on one side, and it had three ribs in its mouth between its teeth. It was told, “Get up and eat your fill of flesh!”
After that, as I watched, I saw another beast, like a leopard. On its back it had four wings like a bird’s, and the beast had four heads. It was given authority to rule.
After that, in my visions at night, I saw a fourth beast, terrifying, frightening and very strong. It had huge iron teeth. It devoured and crushed its victims, and trampled what was left under its feet. It was unlike all the beasts before it, and it had ten horns.
While I was studying the horns, another horn, a small one, grew up among them, and three of the earlier horns were pulled up by the roots to make room for it. This horn had eyes like a human’s eyes and a mouth that spoke boastfully.
As I watched, thrones were put in place,
and the Ancient of Days was seated.
His clothes were white as snow, and the hair of his head like clean wool.
His throne was flames of fire,
and its wheels were blazing fire.
A river of fire was streaming out, flowing from his presence.
Thousands upon thousands served him,
and countless thousands stood before him.
The court was seated, and the books were opened.
I kept watching because of the boastful words the horn was speaking. As I watched, the beast was put to death, and its body was destroyed and thrown into the blazing fire.
The other beasts had their authority taken away, but they were allowed to go on living for a set period of time.
As I watched in the visions of the night,
I saw one like a son of man
coming with the clouds of heaven.
He came to the Ancient of Days
and was presented before him.
He was given authority, glory and kingly power,
so that all peoples, nations and languages would serve him.
His authority is an everlasting authority that will never pass away,
and his kingdom will never be destroyed.

The meaning of the vision

I, Daniel, was deeply troubled in spirit, and the visions that passed through my mind frightened me. I went up to one of those standing there and asked him what all this really meant. So he told me the meaning of these things: “These four great beasts are four kings who will rise up from the earth. But the holy ones of the Most High will receive the kingdom and hold it as their own forever, for ever and ever.” Then I wanted to know what the fourth beast meant, the one that was different from all the others and so terrifying, with its iron teeth and bronze claws, that devoured and crushed its victims and trampled what was left under its feet. I wanted to know as well about the ten horns on its head, and about the other horn that came up, when three of them fell before it. That horn had eyes and a mouth that spoke boastfully, and it looked more imposing than the others. As I watched, this horn was waging war against the holy ones and was defeating them, until the Ancient of Days came and gave judgment in favor of the holy ones of the Most High. Then the time came for the holy ones to take possession of the kingdom. He said this to me: “The fourth beast is a fourth kingdom that will rise on earth. It will be different from all the other kingdoms. It will devour the whole earth, trampling it down and crushing it. The ten horns are ten kings who will arise from this kingdom. After them another king will arise, different from the earlier ones, and he will bring down three kings. He will speak against the Most High and wear down the holy ones of the Most High. He will try to change the sacred times and the law, and they will be handed over to him for a time, two times and half a time. But the court will sit in judgment, and his authority will be taken away, to be completely and finally destroyed. Then the kingdom and the authority and the greatness of all the kingdoms under heaven will be given to the people of the holy ones of the Most High. Their kingdom will last forever, and every ruler will serve and obey them.” This is the end of the account. As for me, Daniel, my thoughts terrified me, and the color drained from my face, but I kept the matter to myself.

fields.title: Daniel 8
fields.body_html:
The ram and the goat

In the third year of King Belshazzar’s reign, I, Daniel, had a vision, after the one I had seen earlier. In the vision I saw myself in the fortress city of Susa, in the province of Elam. In the vision I was beside the Ulai Canal. I looked up and saw a ram standing beside the canal. It had two long horns, one of them longer than the other, and it was the longer one that grew up last. I watched the ram butting toward the west, the north and the south. No animal could stand against it, and no one could rescue anything from its power. It did whatever it wanted and became great. As I was thinking about this, a male goat suddenly came from the west, crossing the whole earth without touching the ground. The goat had a prominent horn between its eyes. It came up to the two-horned ram that I had seen standing beside the canal, and charged at it with furious strength. I saw it reach the ram. It was furious with it, struck the ram and broke both its horns. The ram had no strength to stand against it. The goat threw it to the ground and trampled on it, and no one could rescue the ram from its power. The male goat became very great, but at the height of its power the great horn was broken off. In its place four prominent horns came up, pointing toward the four winds of heaven. Out of one of them came another horn, which started small but grew very great, toward the south and the east and toward the beautiful land. It grew until it reached the host of heaven, and it threw some of the host and some of the stars down to the earth and trampled on them. It even set itself up against the Prince of the host. It took away the regular offering from him, and the place of his sanctuary was overthrown. Because of rebellion, the host will be handed over to it, together with the regular offering. It will throw truth to the ground, and it will succeed in all it does. Then I heard a holy one speaking, and a second holy one asked the one who spoke, “How long will the vision last: the regular offering taken away, the rebellion that brings ruin, and the sanctuary and the host given over to be trampled?” He said to me, “For 2,300 evenings and mornings. Then the sanctuary will be restored to its proper state.” As I, Daniel, watched the vision and tried to make sense of it, someone who looked like a man suddenly stood in front of me. And I heard a human voice from between the banks of the Ulai calling, “Gabriel, explain the vision to this man.” He came near the place where I was standing, and when he came I was terrified and fell face down. But he said to me, “Understand, son of man, that the vision concerns the time of the end.” While he was speaking to me, I sank into a deep sleep, face down on the ground. Then he touched me and raised me to my feet. He said, “I am going to tell you what will happen later, in the time of wrath, for the vision concerns the appointed time of the end. The two-horned ram that you saw stands for the kings of Media and Persia. The shaggy goat is the king of Greece, and the large horn between its eyes is its first king. The four horns that came up in place of the one that was broken are four kingdoms that will arise from his nation, but not with his power. In the last part of their rule, when the rebels have run their full course, a king will arise who is fierce-looking and skilled in intrigue. He will become very strong, but not by his own power. He will cause terrible destruction, and he will succeed in all he does. He will destroy powerful people and the people of the holy ones. By his cunning he will make deceit succeed under his rule. He will make himself great in his own mind, and destroy many who feel secure. He will even rise up against the Prince of princes, but he will be broken, though not by human hands. The vision of the evenings and mornings that has been told to you is true. But keep the vision secret, for it concerns a time far in the future.” I, Daniel, was worn out and lay ill for several days. Then I got up and went about the king’s business. But I was dismayed by the vision; it was beyond understanding.

fields.title: Daniel 9
fields.body_html:
Daniel’s prayer and the seventy sevens

It was in the first year of Darius son of Ahasuerus, a Mede by descent, who had been made king over the realm of the Chaldeans. In the first year of his reign, I, Daniel, came to understand from the scriptures the number of years that, according to the word of the LORD to the prophet Jeremiah, must pass before the desolation of Jerusalem would come to an end: seventy years. So I turned to the Lord God, seeking him in prayer and pleading for mercy, with fasting, in sackcloth and ashes. I prayed to the LORD my God and confessed, saying, “Lord, the great and awesome God, who keeps his covenant and his loyal love with those who love him and keep his commandments, We have sinned and done wrong; we have been wicked and have rebelled, turning away from your commandments and your rules. We did not listen to your servants the prophets when they spoke in your name to our kings, our officials and our ancestors, and to all the people of the land. Lord, righteousness belongs to you, but to us belongs open shame, as it is today: to the people of Judah, the residents of Jerusalem and all Israel, near and far away, in all the lands where you have scattered them because of the unfaithfulness they have shown you. LORD, open shame belongs to us, to our kings, our officials and our ancestors, because we have sinned against you. But the Lord our God is merciful and forgiving, even though we have rebelled against him. We have not obeyed the LORD our God or lived by the instructions he set before us through his servants the prophets. All Israel has broken your law and turned away, refusing to obey you. So the curse and the oath that are written in the law of Moses, the servant of God, have been poured out on us, because we have sinned against him. He has carried out the warnings he spoke against us and against our rulers who governed us, by bringing on us a great disaster. Nowhere under heaven has anything been done like what was done to Jerusalem. All this disaster has come on us, as the law of Moses says it would. Yet we have not pleaded for the favor of the LORD our God by turning away from our sins and paying attention to your truth. So the LORD kept the disaster ready and brought it on us, for the LORD our God is righteous in everything he does, yet we have not obeyed him. Now, Lord our God, you rescued your people from the land of Egypt with a mighty hand and made a name for yourself that lasts to this day. We have sinned; we have done wrong. Lord, in keeping with all your righteous acts, turn your anger and your fury away from your city Jerusalem, your holy mountain. Because of our sins and the wrongdoing of our ancestors, Jerusalem and your people have become an object of scorn to all the nations around us. Now, our God, listen to the prayer and the pleas of your servant. For your own sake, Lord, look with favor on your sanctuary, which lies in ruins. Turn your ear to us, my God, and hear. Open your eyes and see our ruins and the city that bears your name. We do not bring our pleas to you because we are righteous, but because of your great mercy. Lord, listen! Lord, forgive! Lord, take note and act! Do not delay, my God, for your own sake, since your city and your people bear your name.” While I was still speaking and praying, confessing my sin and the sin of my people Israel, and bringing my plea before the LORD my God on behalf of the holy mountain of my God, while I was still praying, Gabriel came to me in swift flight about the hour of the evening offering. He was the man I had seen in the earlier vision. He explained things to me and said, “Daniel, I have now come to give you insight and understanding. As soon as you began to plead, an answer was given, and I have come to tell it to you, for you are greatly loved. So pay attention to the message and understand the vision. Seventy sevens have been decreed for your people and your holy city, to put an end to rebellion, to bring sin to a close, to atone for wrongdoing, to bring in everlasting righteousness, to put a seal on vision and prophecy, and to anoint a most holy place. Know and understand this: from the time the word goes out to restore and rebuild Jerusalem until an anointed leader comes, there will be seven sevens. Then for sixty-two sevens it will be rebuilt, with streets and a trench, but in troubled times. After the sixty-two sevens an anointed one will be cut off, left with nothing. The people of the ruler who is to come will destroy the city and the sanctuary. Its end will come like a flood, and war will continue to the end; desolations have been decreed. He will make a firm covenant with many for one seven. In the middle of the seven he will put a stop to sacrifice and offering. And on a wing of the temple will be the abomination that brings ruin, until the end that has been decreed is poured out on the one who brings ruin.”

fields.title: Daniel 10
fields.body_html:
A vision by the Tigris

In the third year of the reign of Cyrus king of Persia, a message was made known to Daniel, who had been given the name Belteshazzar. The message was true, and it was about a great war. He understood the message; he was given understanding in the vision. At that time I, Daniel, had been mourning for three whole weeks. I ate no fine food; no meat or wine passed my lips, and I did not put any oil on myself until the three weeks were over.

The man clothed in linen

On the twenty-fourth day of the first month, I was beside the great river, the Tigris. I looked up and saw a man dressed in linen, wearing around his waist a belt of fine gold from Uphaz. His body shone like chrysolite, his face like lightning, his eyes like flaming torches, and his arms and legs gleamed like polished bronze. His voice sounded like the noise of a great crowd. I, Daniel, was the only one who saw the vision. The men who were with me did not see it, but such terror came over them that they ran away and hid. So I was left alone, gazing at this great vision. I had no strength left; my face turned deathly pale, and I was helpless. Then I heard him speaking, and as I listened to the sound of his words, I fell into a deep sleep, face down, with my face to the ground. Then a hand touched me and raised me, trembling, onto my hands and knees. He said to me, “Daniel, you are greatly loved. Pay attention to the words I am about to speak to you, and stand up, for I have been sent to you.” When he said this to me, I stood up, trembling. Then he said to me, “Do not be afraid, Daniel. From the first day that you set your mind to gain understanding and humbled yourself before your God, your words were heard, and it is in answer to them that I have come. But the prince of the kingdom of Persia stood in my way for twenty-one days, until Michael, one of the chief princes, came to my aid, because I had been left there alone with the kings of Persia. Now I have come to help you understand what will happen to your people in the days to come, for the vision concerns a time yet to come.” While he was saying these things to me, I bowed with my face toward the ground and could not speak. Then one who looked like a human being touched my lips, and I opened my mouth and began to speak. I said to the one standing in front of me, “My lord, the vision has overwhelmed me with anguish, and I have no strength left. How can I, your servant, speak with you, my lord? My strength is gone, and I can hardly breathe.” Again the one who looked like a human being touched me and gave me strength. He said, “Do not be afraid, you who are greatly loved. Peace be with you. Be strong; be strong!” As he spoke to me, I grew stronger and said, “Speak, my lord, for you have given me strength.” He said, “Do you know why I came to you? Now I must return to fight against the prince of Persia, and when I am done with him, the prince of Greece will come. But first I will tell you what is written in the book of truth. No one supports me against them except Michael, your prince.

fields.title: Daniel 11
fields.body_html:
The kings of the north and the south

“In the first year of Darius the Mede, I myself took my stand to support and strengthen him. Now I will tell you what is true. Three more kings will come to power in Persia, and a fourth will become far richer than any of them. Once his riches have made him strong, he will rouse everyone against the kingdom of Greece. Then a mighty king will arise who will rule a vast empire and do whatever he wants. But at the height of his power his kingdom will be broken up and divided toward the four winds of heaven. His descendants will not inherit it, and it will not have the power he had, for his kingdom will be uprooted and given to others. The king of the south will become strong, and so will one of his officials, who will grow even stronger than he is and will rule; his empire will be great. After some years they will become allies. The king of the south will send his daughter to the king of the north to seal an agreement, but she will not keep her power, and he and his power will not last. She will be handed over, together with her escort, her father, and the one who supported her in those days. One from her family line will rise up in his place. He will attack the army of the king of the north, enter his fortress, fight against them and win. He will also carry off to Egypt their gods, their metal images and their precious objects of silver and gold. For some years he will leave the king of the north alone. Then the king of the north will invade the realm of the king of the south, but will go back to his own country. His sons will prepare for war and gather a great army. One of them will advance like a flood and sweep through, and then again carry the war as far as the enemy’s fortress. Then the king of the south will be enraged and will march out to fight against the king of the north, who will raise a great army; but that army will be defeated by the king of the south. When the army has been carried off, the king of the south will become proud and will kill tens of thousands, but he will not remain strong. For the king of the north will again raise an army, larger than the first, and after a period of years he will come on with a huge, well-equipped army. In those times many will rise against the king of the south. Violent men among your own people will rebel in an attempt to fulfill the vision, but they will fail. Then the king of the north will come, build siege ramps and capture a fortified city. The forces of the south will be unable to resist; even their best troops will not have the strength to stand. The invader will do as he pleases, and no one will be able to stand against him. He will take his stand in the beautiful land, with the power to destroy it. He will make up his mind to come with the full strength of his kingdom, and he will come to terms with the king of the south. He will give him a young woman as his wife, so as to destroy the kingdom, but the plan will not succeed or help him. Then he will turn to the coastlands and take many of them. But a commander will stop his arrogance and turn his arrogance back on him. After this he will head back to the strongholds of his own country, but he will stumble and fall and be seen no more. His successor will send out a tax collector to maintain the splendor of his kingdom. But within a few years he will be destroyed, though not in anger or in battle. In his place a contemptible man will rise to power, one who was not given the royal honor. He will come in when people feel secure and seize the kingdom through intrigue. Armies will be swept away before him like a flood and destroyed, and so will a leader of the covenant. After an alliance is made with him, he will act deceitfully, and with only a small following he will rise to power. When the richest parts of the province feel secure, he will invade them and do what neither his fathers nor his forefathers ever did. He will hand out plunder, spoil and wealth to his followers, and he will plot against fortresses, but only for a time. He will rouse his strength and courage against the king of the south with a large army. The king of the south will go to war with a very large and powerful army, but he will not be able to stand, because of the plots made against him. Those who eat at his table will bring about his downfall. His army will be swept away, and many will fall in battle. Both kings, with their hearts set on evil, will sit at the same table and lie to each other, but it will come to nothing, for the end will still come at the appointed time. The king of the north will return to his own country with great wealth, but his heart will be against the holy covenant, and he will act against it before returning to his own land. At the appointed time he will come back and invade the south, but the outcome will not be what it was the first time. Ships of Kittim will oppose him, and he will lose heart. He will turn back in fury against the holy covenant and take action. Back home, he will favor those who forsake the holy covenant. His forces will rise up and desecrate the sanctuary, the fortress. They will abolish the regular offering and set up the abomination that brings ruin. Those who violate the covenant he will corrupt by flattery, but the people who know their God will stand firm and take action. The wise among the people will instruct many. But for a time they will fall by the sword and by fire, by captivity and by plunder. When they fall, they will receive a little help, and many will join them who are not sincere. Some of the wise will stumble, so that they may be refined, cleansed and made white until the time of the end, for the end will still come at the appointed time. The king will do whatever he wants. He will exalt himself and make himself greater than every god, and he will say outrageous things against the God of gods. He will succeed until the time of wrath is over, for what has been decided will be done. He will show no regard for the gods of his ancestors, or for the god women love, or for any other god, for he will exalt himself above them all. Instead, he will honor a god of fortresses, a god his ancestors did not know. He will honor him with gold and silver, precious stones and costly gifts. With the help of a foreign god he will attack the strongest fortresses. Those who acknowledge him he will greatly honor; he will make them rulers over many people and give them land as a reward. When the time of the end comes, the king of the south will attack him, and the king of the north will rush against him like a storm with chariots and cavalry and a great fleet of ships. He will invade many countries and sweep through them like a flood. He will also invade the beautiful land, and many will fall. But Edom, Moab and the leaders of the Ammonites will escape from his power. He will reach out his power against many countries, and Egypt will not escape. He will take control of the treasures of gold and silver and all the riches of Egypt, and the Libyans and Cushites will follow in his train. But he will be alarmed by news from the east and the north, and he will set out in a great rage to destroy and wipe out many. He will set up his royal tents between the sea and the beautiful holy mountain. Yet he will come to his end, with no one to help him.

fields.title: Daniel 12
fields.body_html:
The time of the end

“At that time Michael, the great prince who protects your people, will arise. There will be a time of distress such as has not happened from the beginning of the nations until then. But at that time your people will be rescued, everyone whose name is found written in the book. Many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, these to everlasting life, and those to shame and everlasting contempt.

The wise will shine

“Those who are wise will shine like the brightness of the sky, and those who lead many to righteousness, like the stars forever and ever.

Seal up the book

“But you, Daniel, keep these words secret and seal up the book until the time of the end. Many will search here and there, and knowledge will increase.” Then I, Daniel, looked, and there before me stood two others, one on this bank of the river and the other on the opposite bank. One of them asked the man dressed in linen, who stood above the waters of the river, “How long will it be until these astonishing things come to an end?” I heard the man dressed in linen, who was standing above the waters of the river, raise his right hand and his left hand toward heaven and swear by the one who lives forever: “It will be for a time, two times and half a time. Once the power of the holy people has been completely broken, all these things will be fulfilled.” I heard, but I did not understand. So I said, “My lord, how will all this turn out?”

Go your way, Daniel

He said, “Go your way, Daniel, for the words are kept secret and sealed until the time of the end. Many will be purified, made white and refined, but the wicked will go on doing evil. Not one of the wicked will understand, but those who are wise will. From the time that the regular offering is abolished and the abomination that brings ruin is set up, there will be 1,290 days. How blessed is the one who waits and reaches the end of the 1,335 days! As for you, go your way until the end. You will rest, and at the end of the days you will rise to receive your inheritance.”

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
As for you, go your way until the end. You will rest, and at the end of the days you will rise to receive your inheritance.”

— Daniel 12:13

Daniel ends with a word to one old man. He has seen empires rise and fall, served four kings, survived the lions and been shown visions that left him ill and bewildered. He has asked how it will all turn out, and has not been told everything. What he is given instead is a promise: go your way, rest, and rise at the end to receive your inheritance. The book that surveyed the kingdoms of the world comes down at last to one faithful life held safe in God’s hands.

The question the book leaves with you

Daniel asks every reader the question it asked its first readers: who really rules? Nebuchadnezzar thought he did, until he ate grass like cattle. Belshazzar thought he could drink from God’s vessels and praise his own gods, and was weighed and found too light the same night. Darius found that the law he had signed could not save the man he valued, and that God could. Again and again the kings themselves are made to say it: “the Most High rules over human kingdoms”, “his kingdom will never be destroyed.”

And if God rules, the next question is how to live under rulers who do not acknowledge him. Daniel’s answer is neither withdrawal nor surrender. He learns Babylon’s literature, serves its kings honestly, and rises high in its government. But he will not eat what defiles him, and he will not stop praying. His friends will not bow to the statue, “even if he does not” rescue them. Their faith does not depend on a happy ending, and the book insists that a happy ending is coming anyway.

Where the book points

The stone cut without hands, the kingdom that will never be destroyed, the one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven to receive an everlasting kingdom: the New Testament sees all of these fulfilled in Jesus. He called himself the Son of Man, announced that the kingdom of God had come near, and before the high priest claimed the vision of Daniel 7 as his own. He spoke of “the abomination that brings ruin, of which the prophet Daniel spoke” in foretelling the fall of the temple. The Revelation to John borrows Daniel’s beasts, its time, times and half a time, and its picture of one whose hair is white as wool. And Daniel’s promise that those who sleep in the dust will awake is fulfilled, the church believes, in the resurrection of Christ, the firstfruits of those who have died.

Christians still differ over how the visions’ details map onto history, and the book itself counsels patience: the words were “kept secret and sealed until the time of the end.” But they do not differ over its hope.

Where to go from here

Daniel has been loved by preachers for its stories and studied by scholars for its visions, and both are in this library. A few places to begin:

  • On the furnace (Daniel 3). Charles H. Spurgeon’s sermon Consolation in the Furnace (3:25), on the fourth man in the fire.
  • On the writing on the wall (Daniel 5). R. A. Torrey’s sermon Found Wanting (5:25–27).
  • On Daniel’s prayers (Daniel 6 and 9). E. M. Bounds’s chapter “Daniel, the Praying Captive” in Prayer and Praying Men; “Windows Open Toward Jerusalem” in The Prayers Jesus Learned, an Ochorus Original on the lions’ den and the prayer of chapter 9; and the chapter “Confession” in D. L. Moody’s Prevailing Prayer, on Daniel’s confession for his people.
  • On the seventy sevens (Daniel 9). George Whitefield’s “The Righteousness of Christ, an Everlasting Righteousness” (9:24), in Selected Sermons of George Whitefield.
  • On the Son of Man and the coming kingdom (Daniel 7). Justin Martyr’s Dialogue with Trypho, chapters 31–32, which quote Daniel 7 at length and distinguish Christ’s two comings; and Cyril of Jerusalem’s The Catechetical Lectures, Lecture XV, on Christ’s return in glory, which opens with Daniel 7:9.
  • On the end and the resurrection (Daniel 7 and 12). Augustine’s The City of God, Book XX, chapter 23, on what Daniel foretold of the last judgement and the kingdom of the saints, and Book XVIII, chapter 34, on Daniel and Ezekiel; and D. L. Moody’s sermon True Wisdom (12:3), on those who lead many to righteousness.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Daniel in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this book.

Then read Daniel beside Jeremiah, whose seventy years he counted, and Ezekiel, who names a Daniel beside Noah and Job among the righteous (Ezekiel 14:14), and beside the Revelation to John, which takes up his visions. And remember, when the beasts seem to be winning, the promise the angel gave him for all who stay faithful:

“Those who are wise will shine like the brightness of the sky, and those who lead many to righteousness, like the stars forever and ever.

— Daniel 12:3
